title: Units and Dimensions in Mechanics
short_intro: Physical quantities are quantified through standardized units, and their dimensional formulae express dependence on fundamental base quantities. Dimensional analysis ensures equation homogeneity and aids in deriving scaling relations across mechanics.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Fundamental SI units, dimensional formulae of mechanical quantities (torque, work, energy, angular momentum, gravitational constant), and principle of dimensional homogeneity.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Dimensional consistency in complex mechanics, derivation of physical relations (central force, time period of satellite, Coriolis force), and limitations of dimensional analysis.

prerequisites: Definition of fundamental and derived physical quantities
Algebra of exponents and basic calculus

concept_notes.heading: Fundamental and Derived Quantities
bullets: The International System of Units (SI) defines seven base quantities: length (m), mass (kg), time (s), electric current (A), thermodynamic temperature (K), luminous intensity (cd), and amount of substance (mol).
Mechanical quantities are derived from mass [M], length [L], and time [T].
Dimensionless quantities such as strain, angle, and relative density have a dimension of [M^0 L^0 T^0].

concept_notes.heading: Principle of Dimensional Homogeneity
bullets: An equation is physically correct only if the dimensions of every term on both sides of the equation are identical.
Quantities of different dimensions cannot be added or subtracted; they can only be multiplied or divided.
Trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential functions must be entirely dimensionless arguments.

concept_notes.heading: Dimensions of Rotational and Gravitational Quantities
bullets: Angular momentum has the dimensional formula [M L^2 T^{-1}], identical to Planck's constant [h].
Universal gravitational constant (G) has dimensions [M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}] derived from Newton's law of gravitation.
Torque and work share the exact same dimensional formula [M L^2 T^{-2}] though they represent distinct physical concepts.

concept_notes.heading: Applications and Limitations of Dimensional Analysis
bullets: Used for checking the correctness of physical equations and converting units from one system to another.
Cannot determine dimensionless constants (e.g., factors like 1/2 in kinetic energy or 4π in force laws).
Fails if an equation involves more than three independent variables when using only [M], [L], [T].

derivations.title: Time Period of a Simple Pendulum
derivations.conditions: Assuming time period depends on length (l), mass of bob (m), and acceleration due to gravity (g)
steps: Write the proportionality relation: T = k cdot l^a cdot m^b cdot g^c, where k is a dimensionless constant.
Substitute the dimensional formulae: [T^1] = [L]^a cdot [M]^b cdot ([L T^{-2}])^c.
Equate powers of fundamental dimensions [M], [L], and [T] on both sides: For M: b = 0; For L: a + c = 0; For T: -2c = 1.
Solve for exponents: c = -1/2, a = 1/2, b = 0.

derivations.title: Centripetal Force Expression
derivations.conditions: Assuming force depends on mass (m), velocity (v), and radius of circular path (r)
steps: Set up the dimensional equation: F = k cdot m^a cdot v^b cdot r^c.
Substitute dimensions: [M L T^{-2}] = [M]^a cdot ([L T^{-1}])^b cdot [L]^c.
Compare powers: For M: a = 1; For T: -b = -2 implies b = 2; For L: a + b + c = 1.
Substitute a and b into L equation: 1 + 2 + c = 1 implies c = -1.

graphs_and_experiments.title: T^2 versus l Graph for a Simple Pendulum
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line plot of squared time period (T^2) on the y-axis against effective length (l) on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the linear plot gives 4π^2 / g, enabling experimental verification of gravitational acceleration.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in numericals where slope values or proportionality constants are derived.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Log-Log Plot for Dimensional Verification
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Plot of log(T) versus log(l) yielding a straight line with slope equal to 0.5.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms power-law dependence without assuming the proportionality constant beforehand.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Evaluates understanding of power-law scaling and dimensional indices.

graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup of a torsion balance with lead spheres attracting smaller test masses.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Measures extremely small gravitational forces to calculate the value of G.

solved_numericals.question: Find the dimensional formula of universal gravitational constant (G) given the formula F = G(m_1 m_2)/r^2.
solution_steps: Rearrange the formula for G: G =  rac{F cdot r^2}{m_1 m_2}
Substitute dimensions of Force [M L T^{-2}], distance [L^2], and mass [M^2].
Combine exponents: [G] =  rac{[M L T^{-2}] [L^2]}{[M^2]} = [M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}]

solved_numericals.question: If velocity (v), force (F), and time (T) are chosen as fundamental physical quantities, find the dimensional formula of mass.
solution_steps: Let Mass m = F^a cdot v^b cdot T^c.
Substitute dimensions: [M^1] = ([M L T^{-2}])^a cdot ([L T^{-1}])^b cdot [T]^c.
Equate powers: For M: a = 1; For L: a + b = 0 implies b = -a = -1; For T: -2a - b + c = 0.
Solve for c: -2(1) - (-1) + c = 0 implies -2 + 1 + c = 0 implies c = 1.

solved_numericals.question: Check the dimensional consistency of the equation for centripetal acceleration: a = v^3 / r.
solution_steps: Write dimensions of RHS:  rac{[L^3 T^{-3}]}{[L]} = [L^2 T^{-3}].
Compare LHS and [L T^{-2}] with RHS [L^2 T^{-3}]; they do not match.
solved_numericals.answer: Dimensionally inconsistent (Equation is incorrect; correct relation is a = v^2 / r)

assumptions_and_limitations: Dimensional analysis assumes physical laws are independent of the choice of system of units.
It cannot detect dimensionless scaling constants, numerical factors, or additive constants in empirical relations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Quantities with the same dimensions must represent the same physical phenomenon.
common_misconceptions.correct: Torque and work share the dimension [M L T^{-2}], but torque is a vector product and work is a scalar product.
common_misconceptions.why: Dimensional identity does not imply identical tensor rank or physical nature.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An equation that is dimensionally correct is always physically correct.
common_misconceptions.correct: A dimensionally correct equation may still contain incorrect dimensionless multipliers or missing additive terms.
common_misconceptions.why: Dimensional homogeneity is a necessary but not sufficient condition for physical correctness.

quick_revision: Dimensional formula of force is [M L T^{-2}] and energy is [M L^2 T^{-2}].
Gravitational Force: F = G  rac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}
Universal Gravitational Constant (G): [G] = M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}
